source: Wang, Yu, Huang, Huang, Wang, Chen, Lyu (2026) Cloud-OpsBench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Agentic Root Cause Analysis in Cloud Systems
finding: Replayed-snapshot RCA benchmark with ten LLM agents including GPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5-Pro. Right final answers often come without the evidence that would justify them. The gap between outcome and process is large.
numbers: 754 cases, 57 fault types, two workloads, ReAct harness, temperature 0, 20-step cap, no extended thinking. OnlineBoutique: best Joint RCA Accuracy (JRA) 0.76 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) but Evidence Closure Rate (ECR) 0.38; GPT-5 JRA 0.68, ECR 0.21; Claude-Sonnet-4 JRA 0.52, ECR 0.44. TrainTicket: GPT-5 JRA 0.68, ECR 0.15; best ECR of any model 0.25. JRA by difficulty (mean over models): OnlineBoutique 0.73 easy, 0.51 medium, 0.30 hard; TrainTicket 0.67, 0.43, 0.08.
quote: final-answer correctness alone substantially overestimates agents' ability to perform evidence-grounded diagnosis
limits: Snapshot replay, not a live system, so no real-time pressure or action effects. Models are 2025-era, no extended thinking. Failure-mode section is a purposive sample, not prevalence.
agent_relevance: Scoring an agent on the final diagnosis alone hides weak evidence use. A revise or impasse operator should log which evidence supports the current hypothesis and test closure, not just answer correctness.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Cloud-OpsBench, RQ2 redundancy and RQ3 experience reuse
finding: Repeated identical tool calls are a weak-model problem here. Strong models show near-zero redundant calls, so their errors are about evidence use. Giving past successful traces or a runbook helps the outcome but barely changes full evidence closure.
numbers: Redundant Action Rate: GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3.5-Plus, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Claude-Sonnet-4 about 0.00 on both workloads; Qwen3-8B 0.46 RAR at 16.01 steps with JRA 0.19; Qwen3-14B 0.28 RAR at 14.58 steps. Experience reuse (3 models, OnlineBoutique): mean JRA 0.70 base, 0.79 with 3 trajectory demos (ICL), 0.76 with runbook (SOP); ECR 0.39 to 0.59 and 0.61. TrainTicket: JRA 0.58 base, 0.56 ICL, 0.62 SOP; ECR 0.18, 0.18, 0.17.
limits: Three cost-efficient models only for RQ3. Retrieval was by symptom, so one symptom maps to many root causes. Experience pool built from GPT-5 successes on a 1:1 train/test split of the same fault families.
agent_relevance: Boundary on the earlier loop findings (AIOpsLab 2024, GPT-3.5): in 2025 strong models do not loop on identical calls in this setting. A repeat-count detector is mostly a guard for weak models. For strong models the impasse is anchoring, which a repeat counter cannot see.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Cloud-OpsBench, section 4.5 failure modes
finding: Authors read failed runs (JRA = 0) from all ten models. Four forms: evidence-grounding failures (anchoring on a loud downstream symptom, ignoring a manifest error already seen, treating an empty result as no evidence), confusion of close mechanisms, and tool-grounding failures (a wrong port gives a real failure that the agent then blames on production).
numbers: Qualitative. Examples: startup events already show manifest unknown, 403 or a missing secret, yet the agent keeps checking peripheral resources; agent anchors on frontend 503 or a CPU alert and blames the noisiest component.
limits: Purposive sample. The paper says it does not estimate prevalence or give an exhaustive taxonomy.
agent_relevance: A direct LLM analogue of fixation and of misread absence of signal. Suggests two checks for the revise step: does the current cause explain the earliest error seen, and was an empty result treated as a finding.

source: Clark, Su, Pial, Tian, Gniedziejko, Jacobsen, Chen, Xu (2026) SREGym: A Live Benchmark for AI SRE Agents with High-Fidelity Failure Scenarios (v3)
finding: Live fault-injection benchmark, 90 problems with ambient noise and metastable and correlated failures. Three agents (Stratus, Claude Code, Codex) with Sonnet-4.6, Kimi K2.5, GPT-5.4. Noise cuts diagnosis for every pair. New failure types are much harder than problems ported from AIOpsLab and ITBench.
numbers: Diagnosis 38.1% to 72.6%, mitigation 40.4% to 78.5% across pairs. Claude Code + Sonnet-4.6: diagnosis 72.6% (62.6% with noise), mitigation 75.6%, end-to-end 60.7% (53.7%). Codex + GPT-5.4: diagnosis 70.0% (59.3%), end-to-end 53.3% (45.9%). Stratus + Sonnet-4.6: diagnosis 61.5% (51.5%), mitigation 78.5%, end-to-end 54.8%. End-to-end on ported problems (n=34) vs new failures (n=13): Stratus 63.7% to 17.9%, Claude Code 60.8% to 28.2%, Codex 57.8% to 15.4%.
limits: Small cell (13 new-failure problems). Table symbols were lost in text extraction, so which row of each pair is the noisy run was taken from the text (diagnosis drops under noise). One setting per pair.
agent_relevance: First 2026 evidence that the detect-to-fix gap and noise sensitivity persist for frontier models. Test the schema on injected-noise cases, not only single-fault ones.

source: Clark et al. (2026) SREGym, appendix D.3 greedy diagnosis
finding: All evaluated agents take the first plausible anomaly as the target, even when it is injected noise or a pre-existing low memory limit. In one problem neither Stratus nor Claude Code ever inspected the faulty frontend. In another, the agent saw evidence for the true cause (password-setting command; health check passing while the app-level connection failed) and still defaulted to the memory story.
numbers: Reported across all runs of Stratus and Claude Code on missing_env_variable_astronomy_shop. valkey_auth_disruption: agent named requirepass as a candidate several times in one run but kept the memory explanation. No prevalence rate given.
quote: the agent treats the first plausible abnormality as a stopping criterion
limits: Case studies chosen by the authors; no count of how many runs fixated. The human comparison (a human would form several hypotheses at once) is stated, not measured.
agent_relevance: This is the fixation pattern in 2026 agents, in the authors' words, with the stopping rule named. Impasse idea: a written root cause must not end the search; require one rival hypothesis and one test that could separate them before acting.

source: Clark et al. (2026) SREGym, section 3.3 diagnosis vs mitigation
finding: Correct diagnosis helps mitigation but is not required. Agents with a wrong first diagnosis often still fix the fault by seeing that the failure persists and trying again.
numbers: P(mitigation | correct diagnosis) 68% to 89%; P(mitigation | wrong diagnosis) 22% to 62%; drop 25 to 46 points. Stratus + Sonnet-4.6 without noise: 3.82 mitigation attempts when diagnosis was wrong vs 1.88 when right.
limits: The benchmark does not tell the agent whether its diagnosis is right. Some mitigations are pattern-matched fixes without understanding.
agent_relevance: Supports a revise trigger based on the symptom persisting after an action (outcome did not change), not only on contradicting evidence. Cheap to compute in code.

source: Clark et al. (2026) SREGym, token cost and tool usage (section 3.1, appendix E)
finding: Stratus, an SRE agent that preprocesses observability data before prompting, used far fewer tokens than the coding agents. It did not match Claude Code on diagnosis.
numbers: Claude Code used 1.81x the tokens per run of Stratus with the same model (Sonnet-4.6); Codex at least 2.44x. Mean tokens: Stratus 812K (464K), Claude Code 1.47M (1.71M), Codex 1.98M (1.88M); first value is the run listed first in the table, second is the other noise condition. Diagnosis: Stratus 61.5% vs Claude Code 72.6%.
limits: Agents differ in many ways besides preprocessing (tools, undo-and-retry, prompts), so this is not a clean test of code-side summaries at equal tokens. Gap 9 is only partly answered.
agent_relevance: Code-side summarising lowers cost but is not shown to raise accuracy. Do not claim a gain from fixed-size records without an equal-token test.

source: Artificial Analysis and IBM (2026) ITBench-AA launch article
finding: Independent re-run of ITBench SRE tasks with one harness (Stirrup) and a 100-turn cap. Longer investigations did not help. Over-investigating models list upstream causes and symptoms as root causes and lose precision.
numbers: 59 tasks x 3 repeats. Claude Opus 4.7 (max effort) 47%, $5.38 per task; GPT-5.5 (xhigh) 46%, 31 turns; Qwen3.7 Max 42%; GLM-5.1 40%; DeepSeek V4 Pro 38%; Gemma 4 31B 37%; Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview 30%, 83 turns. Score is 0 if any ground-truth root cause is missed, else precision.
limits: Vendor article, not peer reviewed. Only some turn counts and costs are given. The scoring punishes extra entities, which favours terse answers.
agent_relevance: Current frontier scores on a fault-management set are below 50%. Turn count is not a quality signal: tune the step cap and stop rule, do not remove them.

source: Wang, Lyu, He, Yang, Zhong, Harel, Lo (2026) Fail-Fast, Restart-Smart: Early Failure Prediction and Restart for SWE Agentic Tasks, Table 1
finding: A 0.6B text-only monitor predicts from the observable prefix that a run will fail. The false-positive budget is set by threshold calibration and swept from 5% to 25%. Two baselines: AgentStop (needs log-probabilities) and Duration, a step-count-only control that a code counter could implement.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified, Qwen3.6-27B. At 5% FPR: FailFast recall 30.5%, precision 76.1%, tokens saved 20.4%; AgentStop 21.0%, 68.6%, 12.5%; Duration 19.8%, 67.3%, 11.4%. At 25% FPR: FailFast recall 68.3%, precision 58.8%, saved 49.0%; AgentStop 54.5%, 52.3%, 37.2%; Duration 50.9%, 51.8%, 33.7%. On Qwen3.5-9B at 5% FPR the three tie (recall 34.7, 35.1, 34.7). Closed Gemini 3 Flash: FailFast recall 22.7% at 5% and 44.8% at 25%, Duration 17.8% and 32.5%.
limits: Monitor is learned on same-family trajectories. No repeat-action or no-new-evidence counter was tested. Failed runs are longer, so step count is a late signal, and it only helps at fixed false-alarm rates the authors choose.
agent_relevance: Closest data on gap 1. A rule that uses only the step count already catches a large share of failing runs. A learned monitor adds modest recall at the same false-alarm rate. There is still no ablation of detector vs no detector for a code counter against a model-judged stuck flag at equal tokens.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Fail-Fast, Restart-Smart, Table 3 restart strategies
finding: After an alarm, a fresh rollout with no prior history (cold restart) adds almost nothing. A fresh rollout that is also offered the interrupted run's code diff as an optional overlay does better and loses fewer runs that would have passed. A prompt-level intervention helps a weak model and hurts a strong one.
numbers: Baseline resolve rates: Qwen3.5-9B 48.2, Qwen3.6-27B 66.6, Gemma4-31B 62.2. Qwen3.6-27B at 25% FPR: RestartSmart 71.8 (+5.2), cold restart 66.8 (+0.2). Qwen3.5-9B at 10% FPR: 52.2 (+4.0) vs 50.8 (+2.6). Would-have-passed runs lost to false alarms on Qwen3.6-27B: cold restart 36.4% (10% FPR) and 27.5% (25%) vs 15.2% and 8.8% with overlay. Net token overhead +43.8% vs +18.2% at 25%. SWE-PRM prompt feedback: +4.2 on the 9B model, -3.2 on the 27B.
limits: One benchmark (SWE-bench Verified), single runs per setting, 2026 open models. The overlay is code state, a domain-specific carry-over.
agent_relevance: Fresh-context restart alone is weak evidence for gap 3. What crosses the boundary matters. Carry over verified facts and partial work, not the old reasoning. False alarms are costly without carry-over.

source: Wei, Ni, Zhao, Gan, Cohan (2026) Step-level Optimization for Efficient Computer-use Agents
finding: A learned Stuck Monitor, reading the last K reasoning-action steps, triggers escalation to a stronger model. Compared with the small model alone, with each monitor on or off, and with a fixed-interval check every k steps.
numbers: OSWorld: EvoCUA-8B alone 43.3%; with both monitors plus Kimi K2.5 58.2% at $0.051 per task vs $0.022 small and $0.132 for Kimi alone (60.1%). WebArena: AgentTrek-32B alone 30.3%, with both monitors plus GPT-5.2 58.8%; gpt-oss-20b 37.6% to 57.8%. Fixed-interval checks (k in 3, 5, 7, best shown): OSWorld 55.1% at $0.07 vs event-driven 58.2% at $0.05; WebArena 52.5% at $0.24 vs 58.8% at $0.21. Stuck detector held-out accuracy 93.9%, F1 91.5% (teacher GPT-5.2: 96.5%, 92.7%).
limits: No-detector means the small model alone, so the gain mixes detection with a stronger model taking over. It is not a same-model recovery test. Stuck-only and milestone-only values could not be read reliably from the figure; the text says either alone beats no detector and both is best. Labels come from an LLM teacher.
agent_relevance: Event-driven checks beat fixed-interval ones at lower cost (a partial answer to gap 4: three fixed rates tried, none optimal). Loops and oscillation are what the stuck flag finds.

source: Gumaan (2026) Feedback That Backfires: Why Small Language Model Agents Repeat the Call They Just Watched Fail
finding: Putting a failed call and its error in the transcript raises the chance of repeating the call, for six small instruction-tuned models. The failed call's surface text does most of the damage. A written 'do not repeat' does not change it. Deleting the failed step and retrying from a clean context gave the highest repeat rate under greedy decoding.
numbers: 6 models, 135M to 1.7B, 4 families. About -1.03 nats per action token, odds factor 2.8; holds on 90% to 100% of items. Probability of the failed call among 4 candidates 0.06 to 0.54; greedy repeats it token for token on 19% of items vs 0% before. Surface form is 83% of the damage. A runtime-made description of the failure removes 76% of the inversion. ToolShed rollouts (Qwen2.5-0.5B, 24 tasks): exact repeat rate 31% standard, 24% with the instruction, 80% with clean restart (+49 points, CI +33 to +64), task success -8 (CI -21 to +0).
quote: the context after a failure must differ from the context before it, and the difference must not be the failed action
limits: Tiny models (up to 1.7B), 24 rollout tasks, greedy decoding. With sampling a restart would add variation. Not shown for frontier models.
agent_relevance: Do not paste the failed action text back; record the failure as a code-made description. A clean restart with the same context under greedy decoding repeats the same move. Test before relying on this for large models.

source: Yang (2026) Context-Contaminated Restart Model (seen through a search summary and a blog)
finding: Model of retries where the context keeps earlier failed attempts, so later attempts fail more often. Fitted to SWE-bench Verified. Claim is that clearing context before a retry is optimal.
numbers: As relayed: error rate 0.034 clean vs 0.239 contaminated, ratio 7.1; an independent-retry model overestimates pass@3 by 17.4 points (98.6% predicted vs 81.2% observed).
limits: Paper not opened; numbers come from a search summary and a secondary blog. Treat as unverified. Gumaan (d12) and Wang (d10) both qualify the clear-the-context advice.
agent_relevance: Marks the opposing view (clear the context). Evidence now says clear-and-nothing-else is weak.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Where LLM Agents Fail and How They can Learn From Failures (AgentDebug)
finding: Taxonomy of module-level errors, 200 annotated failure trajectories, and a debugger that finds the earliest root-cause step. Large gain in step localization over direct prompting, but weak absolute accuracy.
numbers: AgentErrorBench: 100 ALFWorld, 50 WebShop, 50 GAIA trajectories, 10 annotators, Cohen kappa 0.55. Averages: step accuracy 45.0% vs direct prompting 28.0%; step+module 31.3% vs 10.0%; all-correct 24.3% vs 0.3% (brute force 0.0%, binary search 0.3%). GAIA step accuracy 58.0% vs 30.0%. Downstream ALFWorld success, first attempt to re-rollout from the found step: GPT-4o-mini 21 to 55, Qwen3-8B 48 to 74, Qwen3-Next-80B 60 to 84 (baselines token-matched).
limits: Detector is GPT-4.1 with a long structured prompt and the taxonomy. No independent replication found. The all-correct bar (step, module and error type) is strict, so the baseline is near zero. Kappa 0.55 is called substantial by the authors and moderate on common scales.
agent_relevance: Even the best localizer misses the root-cause step more than half the time (45.0%). Use localization as a hint to re-check a step, not as a verdict.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? (Who&When): length and random baselines
finding: Failure attribution gets worse with longer logs and falls near zero at the longest. Random guessing is a high bar on short, algorithm-made logs.
numbers: Hand-crafted systems split into 5 length levels: 5-17, 19-29, 31-49, 51-91, 93-130 steps; all three methods decline with length and step-level accuracy is more sensitive. Algorithm-generated systems have at most 10 steps. Random baseline step-level 19.06% (algorithm-generated) and 4.16% (hand-crafted); agent-level 29.10% and 12.00%. With a tolerance of 5 steps, hand-crafted step-level accuracy is 33.6% to 37.1% across methods.
limits: One decisive error per log. The table text lost its layout, so only baselines and length ranges are quoted. Models are 2025 GPT-4o and others.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 6: AgentDebug trajectories (ALFWorld, WebShop, GAIA) are probably shorter and more structured, where localization is easier. Who&When shows the length effect. No source tests this directly or replicates AgentDebug. Keep K21 contested.

source: DeAnda and Gaba (1990) Unplanned incidents during comprehensive anesthesia simulation, Anesth Analg
finding: First- and second-year residents in a full simulator. Recordings were coded for unplanned incidents. Fixation errors were a fifth of incidents.
numbers: 19 simulations, 132 unplanned incidents; 73% simple, 27% critical. Human error 65.9% (87 incidents), fixation errors 20.5% (27 incidents, 0 to 3 per simulation, mean 1.42), equipment failure 3% (4), unknown 10.6%. Resident groups differed overall (P less than 0.025).
limits: The unit is share of incidents, not share of people, so it cannot be set beside Schwid and O'Donnell's 63% of subjects. The coding rule for fixation is not in the abstract. Small sample, residents only.
agent_relevance: A second independent human rate for fixation from a different group and simulator, so K01 now has two sources. Different units: report them separately.

source: Schwid and O'Donnell (1992) Anesthesiologists' management of simulated critical incidents, Anesthesiology
finding: Computer-based simulator; ten residents, ten faculty and ten private-practice anesthesiologists. Fixation or failure to revise a plan when cues disagreed was common. Gathering more information helped in the anaphylaxis case.
numbers: 63% of subjects made fixation errors or failed to revise a plan. Correct anaphylaxis diagnosis 40%; 27% adequately treated myocardial ischemia; 30% managed cardiac arrest to ACLS guideline. All experienced anesthesiologists diagnosed esophageal intubation; 2 residents misread the missing end-tidal CO2.
limits: Abstract only (cut at 250 words), so no per-group split for fixation. PC simulator, no control, and the scoring rule for failure to revise is not given. A search for a replication using the same scoring found none.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open for the 63% figure: no same-scoring replication was found. The rate depends on how failure to revise is coded, which the abstract does not show.

source: Woods and Cook (c. 1999) Perspectives on Human Error: Hindsight Biases and Local Rationality, section on fixation
finding: Defines fixation: the first assessment is reasonable, evidence later points away, and people keep it despite chances to revise. Two criteria: persistence over time and cues available that could have started a revision. Names garden-path problems and the trade-off between fixation and thematic vagabonding. Says a person with a fresh point of view usually breaks a fixation, and lists three remedies: fresh viewpoint, devil's advocate, better process feedback.
numbers: No rates. Cites De Keyser and Woods 1990, Johnson et al. 1981 and 1988, Gaba and DeAnda 1989, Roth, Woods and Pople 1992, Woods et al. 1987 (Three Mile Island), Dorner 1983 for vagabonding.
quote: failures to revise situation assessment as new evidence comes in have been referred to as functional fixations, cognitive lockup and cognitive hysteresis
limits: A review chapter, not the primary studies. De Keyser and Woods (1990) itself and Woods (1994) were not opened. The text says nothing about decompensation, cross purposes or outdated behavior.
agent_relevance: Gives a checkable definition for the detector: persistence plus an available revision cue. Use both tests, not persistence alone, so a hypothesis that is simply right is not flagged.

source: Woods and Branlat (2011) Basic patterns in how adaptive systems fail, in Resilience Engineering in Practice; read through a Wikipedia entry and a search summary
finding: The three patterns (decompensation, working at cross-purposes, getting stuck in outdated behaviors) come from a conceptual chapter on adaptive systems, not from the dynamic fault management studies. Summaries: decompensation is running out of capacity to adapt as challenges cascade faster than responses; cross-purposes is locally adaptive but globally maladaptive action; outdated behavior is keeping once-adaptive strategies after the world changed.
numbers: No counts or rates in any accessible source.
limits: Secondary descriptions only (Wikipedia, slide decks, blog summaries); the chapter text was not opened. Wikipedia gives the year as 2017 while the chapter is in the 2011 Ashgate volume, so the date is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Closes the provenance part of gap 2: there are no measured rates to map to detector rules. Map by mechanism instead: outdated behavior to repeat and persistence rules, decompensation to budget exhaustion, cross-purposes to conflicting sub-goals or agents.

source: Roth, Mumaw and Lewis (1994) NUREG/CR-6208, An Empirical Investigation of Operator Performance in Cognitively Demanding Simulated Emergencies
finding: The report exists (Westinghouse for the NRC, July 1994). It studies the role of situation assessment and diagnosis when operators use emergency procedures.
numbers: Not obtained: nrc.gov returned Access Denied for the PDF and 403 for the page; OSTI would not connect; a NASA slide deck citing it had no counts.
limits: No findings, counts per failure type or crew numbers were read. All content claims are from catalogue descriptions.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 (per-failure-type counts) stays open. Do not cite any rate from this report.

source: Vijayvargiya et al. (2025) Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering
finding: Models almost never ask unless prompted. When asked to judge whether an instruction is underspecified, results swing widely with prompt and model. Interaction raises the resolve rate a lot.
numbers: Up to 74% gain over non-interactive. Claude Sonnet 4 reaches 89% of full-spec performance with interaction; Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Haiku up to 80%; Deepseek 59%; Llama 3.1 54%. Detection (accuracy, false positive, false negative): Sonnet 4 neutral prompt 0.74, 0.08, 0.44; strong-encouragement prompt 0.89, 0.03, 0.18. Qwen 3 Coder 0.50, 0.00, 1.00 at all prompts. Llama 3.1 70B moderate prompt 0.47, 0.95, 0.09.
limits: The user is simulated and holds the full spec; underspecification is made by summarising issues. The 74% is a relative gain.
agent_relevance: Direct data on a model-judged 'should I stop and ask' trigger: false-alarm and miss rates swing from 0 to 1 with prompt wording. Argues for code-side conditions (stall count) to trigger the ask, with the model only writing the question. Supports gap 10 (asking recovers a lot) and gap 7 (false-alarm numbers for a model-judged trigger).

source: Edwards and Schuster (2026) Ask or Assume? Uncertainty-Aware Clarification-Seeking in Coding Agents
finding: A scaffold that separates the underspecification check from the coding agent. The abstract reports a higher resolve rate than a single agent and fewer queries on easy tasks.
numbers: Resolve rate 69.40% for the scaffold; 61.20% for the standard single-agent setup (OpenHands with Claude Sonnet 4.5, as relayed by a search summary).
limits: Abstract read through the arXiv listing only; the 61.20% comes from a search summary.
agent_relevance: A second source that a separate checker beats a single agent judging its own need to ask. Single-source until opened.

source: Testing-Driven Reliability Audit of Trajectory-Based Early Outcome Prediction for LLM Agents (2026)
finding: Audit of whether an early-outcome predictor stays calibrated when applied to an agent it was not trained on. Most agent pairs were fine; two combinations were persistently off.
numbers: Median pairwise corrected-gap differences 0.0180 (SUCCESS head, 45 pairs) and 0.0385 (FAILURE head, 35 pairs); persistent errors for gpt-5-mini/SUCCESS (0.1377) and claude-opus-4.6/FAILURE (0.1107). Did not replicate on TerminalBench.
limits: Abstract only. Concerns calibration, not task success after intervention.
agent_relevance: A detector's false-alarm rate can shift when the agent changes. Recalibrate per model rather than copy a threshold.

source: AgentStop (2026) Terminating Local AI Agents Early to Save Energy in Consumer Devices
finding: A log-probability-based supervisor stops trajectories unlikely to succeed. It saves energy with a small loss of task performance.
numbers: 15% to 20% less wasted energy, under 5% utility drop on web QA and coding benchmarks (abstract).
limits: Abstract only. Needs token log-probabilities, which closed APIs do not expose.
agent_relevance: Cost side of an impasse stop rule. Compare with d09, where AgentStop is a baseline.
